transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what's been going on that brought you in today?

Well, I'm here because... I just can't seem to get anything done anymore. I spend practically my whole day just going back over the same things in the house. You know, checking the outlets, making sure the locks are turned right, messing with my tools... 

Speaking of tools, I used to have this really great Craftsman wrench set back when I was still working. My buddy Dave gave it to me. Dave actually moved out to Ohio a few years back, bought a farm out there. He always said he wanted to raise alpacas, which is kind of funny because he's absolutely terrified of dogs, so I don't know how he handles the farm animals, but anyway... 

What was I saying? Oh, right. The house. Yeah, I just keep going over the tools, and checking the locks, and wiping up the dust. Over and over. I'll fix something, and check it, and check it again until I'm just completely worn out. But even when I'm exhausted, I still don't feel sure enough to just leave it alone. It's taking up my whole day.
Do you find yourself having thoughts or mental images that come up over and over, even when you don't want them to, and that bother you or make you feel anxious?

Yeah... yeah, I do. It's like, even when I know for a fact I did the job right, these really ugly thoughts just keep jumping into my head. Like I'll fix an outlet and suddenly I'm thinking about a loose wire I might have missed, and I just picture it sparking and burning the whole house down. 

Which would be a total nightmare, especially since our homeowner's insurance just went up again. My wife was on the phone with the insurance guy for like two hours last week trying to get a better rate. The guy's name was Greg, I think. Or maybe Craig? He sounded like a Craig. He kept trying to sell us on this bundle with the auto insurance, but we don't even drive that much since I'm not working right now. I mostly just stay at the house. But anyway, Craig or Greg or whatever, he couldn't get the price down, so he was pretty much useless. 

But... what was I saying? Oh, the thoughts. Right. Yeah, or I'll get this image of a nail I might have left on the floor somewhere, and I just know my wife is going to step on it and get seriously hurt. And I try... I really try to just push those thoughts out of my head, you know? Just tell myself it's fine. But they just come right back even stronger.

When you have those upsetting thoughts, do you feel driven to do something over and over — like checking, counting, or cleaning — to try to make the thoughts go away or to prevent something bad from happening?

Yeah, exactly. That's... that's exactly what it is. When I get that picture in my head of the house burning down or my wife stepping on a nail, I just... I have to go back and check. I'll go back to the outlet, take the cover plate off, check the wires, put it back on. Then I'll do it again. And again. I'm just trying to make that awful feeling stop, you know? To make sure it's safe. 

It's just like how I check the locks. Speaking of locks, I actually installed this new deadbolt on the back door last month. It's one of those smart locks, supposedly. You're supposed to be able to control it from your phone, which sounds great in theory, right? But the app is absolute garbage. It keeps disconnecting from the Wi-Fi. My neighbor, Tom, he's got the same one, and he says his works fine, but Tom also thinks the moon landing was faked, so I don't really trust his judgment on much of anything. He's always out in his yard at like 6 AM with this incredibly loud leaf blower. I don't even know where he gets that many leaves, we don't have that many trees on our street...

Wait, sorry. The checking. Right. Yeah, I just... I spend most of my day going back over the same outlets, the locks, my tools, even wiping up dust over and over. I just keep checking and fixing them, trying to make those thoughts go away, until I'm just completely worn out. But even then, I still don't feel sure enough to just walk away and leave it alone.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms of intrusive, anxiety-provoking thoughts followed by repetitive checking behaviors aimed at reducing distress or preventing a feared event align most closely with obsessive-compulsive disorder. Other candidates (F43.22, F32.1, F32.2) are ruled out due to absence of criteria such as a depressive or stress-related disorder.

inference_history.note: The patient describes repetitive behaviors (checking locks, tools, cleaning) that consume a significant amount of time and cause distress, which points toward a possible obsessive-compulsive disorder (F42.2). However, other differential diagnoses such as generalized anxiety disorder (F43.22), major depressive disorder with anxious features (F32.1/F32.2), adjustment disorder (F54), or other specified neurodevelopmental or neuropsychiatric disorders (F06.4) remain plausible at this stage.
